To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Biotic Ligand Models (BLMs) are not able to predict the metal toxicity over time and that a mechanistic model is required for the prediction of the metal toxicity over the time.

the classical BLM is inadequate to predict metal toxicity over time because of neglecting metal transport dynamics and intracellular metal excretory processes, which can be incorporated in a more rigorous model that is derived here.

(i) metal partitioning at the biointeface during cell exposure is a dynamic and time-dependent process that is controlled by the interplay of metal transport dynamics and cell growth; (ii) metal transport dynamics and metal-induced cell growth are coupled processes that cannot be treated as separate phenomena, and (iii) BLM is not adequate to evaluate metal toxicity over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an integrated mechanistic model of metal partitioning dynamics at biointerfacing and its coupling to cell growth and metal internalisation processes.
the development of a mechanistic model that integrates cell electrostatics with metal partitioning at the cell surface and metal toxicity to microalgae and bacteria.
the formulation of metal partition at biointerface dynamics and metal-induced cell growth-inhibition under steady-state conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Biotic Ligand model (BLM) is not adequate to evaluate metal toxicity to microalgae and bacteria under non-complexed conditions over time.

the BLM is not suitable to describe the dynamics of metal partitioning and toxicity at the biointerior, unless the cell growth inhibition is instantaneous and the metal depletion from bulk is negligible.

the BLM framework should be used with great caution in the interpretation of metal toxicity to microorganism over time, especially when the metal internalisation rate is slow and cell size changes occur.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

metal toxicity to microalgae and bacteria can be significantly underestimated when the BLM is applied under non-steady-state exposure conditions, especially for metal internalisation kinetics that are fast relative to the cell growth kinetics and for cells that have a large initial size and density.
metal toxicity to microalgae and bacteria is a dynamic process where metal transport and metal-induced cell growth are coupled and cannot be treated separately.
a mechanistic understanding of metal partitioning and toxicity dynamics at biointerface requires a coupled formulation of metal transport dynamics and cell growth inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
metal toxicity is a function of the metal transport dynamics to cell surface and the kinetics of cell growth inhibition.
the BLM framework is insufficient to predict metal toxicity to microorganism over time, unless metal partitioning dynamics at the biointersurface is explicitly accounted for.

metal transport dynamics and cell growth inhibition are both essential for a mechanistic understanding of metal toxicity to micro-organisms and that the BLM is inadequate to account for such coupled processes.
